prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

After Cai Guo-Qiang Quick, before the sun rises, get up one more time, my grandmother. The artist won’t mind if you borrow his sky ladder. Place your foot on the bottom rung and keep climbing, even though you’re a skeleton with a broken neck from falling downstairs on Guy Fawkes night. The ladder is wrapped in gunpowder, and he’s lit the touchpaper. Your bones are ascending firecrackers. You’re half a kilometer high now, halfway to the universe, my joy-gardener. I hope you find a garden with rich black soil for your black roses, hybrids like you— half white half Indian, half woman half flower, their roots twined through your skull, you who were transplanted among the pale roses of a British family. Your skin now a mix of photons and soot. What do you find up there? Is there a hothouse? Are there alien hands with deft brushes pollinating stars? Remember how your tomatoes kept yielding more planets? Are there constellations of exotic fruit now you’ve reached the top? Have you gone back enough in space-time to when you were alive? The ladder is charred, the hot air balloon that held it up is about to collapse. The explosions are over. Cai showers his head with champagne, as his 100-year-old granny watches on her cell phone.Did you see it? He asks,did you hear the whoosh, the rat-tat-tat at the starry door? You can go back to sleep now

outputs.L2:
After Cai Guo-Qiang

Hurry—before dawn breaks, rise once more, grandmother. The artist will not object if you make use of his ladder to the sky. Set one foot on the lowest step and go on upward, though you are only bones now, your neck broken from that fall down the stairs on Guy Fawkes night.

The ladder has been bound with gunpowder, and the fuse is already burning. Your skeleton climbs in a burst of firecrackers. Now you are five hundred metres above the ground, midway toward the universe, my gardener of joy.

I wish for you a garden there, one with deep, dark earth for your black roses—crossbreeds like yourself: part white, part Indian; part woman, part blossom. Their roots wind through your skull, you who were once set down among the pale roses of a British household. Your skin has become a mingling of light-particles and ash.

What is waiting for you at that height? A greenhouse? Strange hands, skilled with tiny brushes, fertilising the stars? Do you remember how your tomato plants never stopped producing more little worlds? Now that you have reached the summit, are there clusters of unfamiliar fruits arranged like constellations? Have you travelled far enough back through space and time to arrive again in your living days?

The ladder is blackened. The hot-air balloon that kept it suspended is close to failing. The detonations have finished. Cai pours champagne over his own head while his hundred-year-old grandmother watches through her mobile phone.

Did you see it? he asks. Did you hear the rush, the rapid crackling at the door of the stars?

You may sleep again now.
outputs.L3:
The poem imagines the speaker’s deceased grandmother ascending Cai Guo-Qiang’s fiery artwork, the “sky ladder,” in the moments before sunrise. In this vision, the ladder is not only a spectacle of fire and smoke, but also a passage between worlds. The grandmother appears as a fragile skeleton, rising slowly through bursts of flame and explosions. Yet the violence of the image becomes strangely tender: as she climbs, she is transformed into fire, brightness, and motion, as though death itself is being remade into light.

The speaker connects this imagined ascent to the grandmother’s identity and earthly life. Her mixed heritage is evoked through images of black roses and rich soil, suggesting both beauty and rootedness, as well as histories buried deep in the body and the land. Her love of gardening also shapes the poem’s imagery. Tomatoes, dirt, flowers, and seeds become part of the grandmother’s presence, showing her as someone who cultivated life even in ordinary places. These garden images gradually expand beyond the earth, linking the domestic and familiar to the cosmic and mysterious.

As the grandmother climbs higher, the poem turns into a fantasy of reaching the universe. The sky becomes a vast garden, where impossible forms of growth might exist: alien pollinators, strange blossoms, and constellations shaped like fruit. The grandmother’s gardening is no longer limited to the ground she once tended; it is imagined on a cosmic scale. In this way, the poem transforms grief into wonder, allowing the speaker to picture an afterlife filled not with stillness, but with cultivation, movement, and radiant possibility.

By the end, the poem returns to Cai Guo-Qiang’s artwork and to the real story behind it: Cai’s own grandmother watching the fiery ladder rise into the sky. This return creates a quiet parallel between the artist’s grandmother and the speaker’s. Both women become connected through the image of the ladder, through memory, and through acts of love offered across generations. Finally, the speaker gently releases their grandmother from the vision, letting her return to sleep. The ending is tender and restrained, suggesting that imagination can briefly summon the dead, lift them into light, and then lovingly let them rest again.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores grief, ancestry, and the imagined afterlife by reimagining Cai Guo-Qiang’s explosive artwork *Sky Ladder* as a visionary path for the speaker’s dead grandmother. In the original artwork, a ladder of fire rises into the sky, both spectacular and temporary. The poem transforms that image into something intimate: not just a public display of artistic daring, but a private, emotional passage between the living and the dead. The ladder becomes a way for the speaker to picture the grandmother’s ascent, giving shape to a longing that cannot otherwise be fulfilled.

Throughout the poem, fiery, botanical, and cosmic imagery blend together to create a surreal landscape of mourning. Fire suggests destruction, ritual, illumination, and release; it burns, but it also guides. Botanical images connect the grandmother to growth, roots, family lineage, and the living earth, emphasizing her place within ancestry and memory. Cosmic imagery expands the poem’s grief beyond the personal, placing the grandmother’s death within a vast universe of stars, sky, and mystery. These images allow the poem to move between the earthly and the celestial, between the body and the spirit, between memory and imagination.

At its heart, the poem is tender rather than despairing. It does not claim to overcome death, but it imagines a momentary bridge across it. By turning *Sky Ladder* into a symbolic route for the grandmother, the speaker finds a way to reconnect with her, if only through art and imagination. The poem suggests that art can briefly suspend the finality of loss: it can make the absent visible, the unreachable near, and the dead newly present in the mind of the living. In this way, the poem becomes both an elegy and an act of devotion, using wonder to soften grief and memory to keep love alive.

After Cai met Guo at the old riverside market, the city no longer felt as lonely as it once had. Cai had arrived with only a small suitcase and a notebook full of plans, hoping to begin again in a place where nobody knew the mistakes of the past. Guo, who ran a quiet tea shop near the bridge, noticed Cai sitting outside each morning, watching the crowds pass by.

At first, their conversations were simple. Guo spoke about the changing seasons, the best tea leaves, and the history of the neighborhood. Cai listened carefully, grateful for the calm rhythm of Guo’s words. After several weeks, Cai began to share stories too—about lost opportunities, difficult choices, and the hope of building a better future.

Guo never offered easy answers. Instead, Guo reminded Cai that life often changes slowly, like tea leaves unfolding in hot water. After hearing this, Cai started to understand that healing did not happen all at once. It came through small acts: waking early, working honestly, trusting another person, and forgiving oneself.

In time, Cai became part of the community. People greeted Cai by name, and the tea shop became a familiar refuge. After everything that had happened, Cai realized that a new beginning was not a single moment, but a journey. And on that journey, Guo’s quiet friendship became one of the most important gifts Cai had ever received.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem titled “After Cai Guo-Qiang” that addresses a dead grandmother, weaving in Cai’s Sky Ladder, fireworks, ancestry, gardening, Guy Fawkes night, and grief.
counterfactuals.output:
**After Cai Guo-Qiang**

Grandmother, tonight I have borrowed a ladder made of fire and leaned it against the dark, as if heaven were only the roof of your old greenhouse, streaked with rain and soot. Cai sent his Sky Ladder upward for his grandmother, and I think of you, your hands smelling of tomatoes and damp twine, the small moon of your thumbnail pressing seeds into soil as though each one were a message to the dead.

On Guy Fawkes night, the gardens detonate. Children cheer at the sky’s brief wounds. Catherine wheels spin like trapped galaxies nailed to fences. Rockets climb, hesitate, and flower into chrysanthemums of gunpowder, red peonies, blue orchids, ancestral weeds. I stand among the cabbages and ash, calling you by the names the family no longer uses, names worn smooth as stones in the mouth. Above me the fireworks write and erase our lineage faster than I can read it.

You always said the dead lived under the beans. That if we kept digging, we would find them: great-grandfathers curled like bulbs, aunties sprouting green hair, the old country folded in a packet of seeds. I did not believe you then. Now every root resembles a finger beckoning. Every worm is a sentence. Every bonfire is an altar where a straw man burns and nobody says whose face we have given him.

Grandmother, if grief is a garden, it has no season. It grows black dahlias in December. It trains ivy through the ribs. It fills the watering can with stars and asks me to pour them over the graves of marigolds. I have tried to prune it, to make it respectable, but at dusk it climbs the walls, luminous and lawless, until the whole house is trellised with longing.

So I light the fuse.

Not to summon you back—no firework can reverse the falling ash, no ladder, however radiant, can remain in the sky. I light it because for one impossible moment the night opens its golden rungs, and I see you above the allotment, kneeling in your apron among constellations, thinning the seedlings of the afterlife. Your face is made of sparks. Your voice is the soft collapse after thunder.

Then darkness returns, carrying the smell of smoke, chrysanthemums, and turned earth. I stand there with my hands full of invisible seeds, waiting for you to tell me where to plant them.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an ekphrastic poem inspired by Cai Guo-Qiang’s Sky Ladder, in a second-person apostrophe to my mixed-race grandmother who loved black roses and tomatoes and died after falling down stairs.
counterfactuals.output:
Grandmother, you would have loved the ladder  
because it was made of fire  
and still wanted to be a way up.

Not Jacob’s, not the attic’s narrow pull-down,  
not the stairs that betrayed your hip,  
your breath, the small basket of laundry  
or tomatoes—who can say what you carried  
when the house tilted its dark mouth open.

This one rose over the harbor at dawn,  
a spine of gunpowder and gold,  
each rung briefly declaring itself  
against the blue body of the sky.  
A dragon of steps. A hymn with teeth.  
A staircase no foot could bruise.

Grandmother, black-rose woman,  
brown-and-ivory woman, woman  
people tried to name in halves—  
you knew how beauty could be bred  
from contradiction: velvet petals  
dark as a closed eye, tomatoes splitting  
their red hearts in your palm, salt  
on the cutting board, summer  
shining through the kitchen screen.

I call to you now as if flame  
could answer blood. As if Cai’s ladder,  
lit and vanishing, had been lowered  
for those who left by falling.  
As if every rung were a second chance  
to rise without weight, without bone,  
without the sudden arithmetic of stairs.

Did you see it from wherever you are—  
that impossible trellis climbing nowhere,  
that bright refusal to remain on earth?  
For a moment the sky accepted it.  
For a moment, fire behaved  
like a garden.

And I thought of your black roses  
opening their midnight fists.  
I thought of tomatoes warm from the vine,  
how you sliced them thick,  
how the knife flashed and was gone.

Grandmother, if I could,  
I would build you a ladder  
that begins at the last step  
and burns backward into morning.  
I would stand below, calling,  
not come down, not yet—  
keep climbing that brief gold road  
until even the ashes forget  
the shape of falling.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyrical, dreamlike paragraph-poem about using an artist’s gunpowder ladder to help a deceased grandmother ascend into the cosmos; include images of bones, flowers, stars, and a final quiet return to sleep.
counterfactuals.output: We carried the artist’s gunpowder ladder into the field at dusk, its black rungs dusted with ash and pollen, and laid it against the blue wall of evening for Grandmother, whose bones had grown light as flower stems beneath the earth. When the fuse took, fire climbed rung by rung, a bright serpent uncoiling toward the stars, and we saw her rise through the sparks in her old white dress, marigolds opening at her feet, her hands full of seeds and moonlit thread. Above us the constellations leaned close like kind faces; below, the soil held its breath around the tender architecture of ribs and roots. She did not look back, or perhaps she did, in the way a star looks back for centuries—softly, without asking to be followed. When the ladder vanished into smoke, petals fell through the dark, warm as embers, and we gathered them from our hair in silence, returned to the house, closed the door on the flowering night, and went quietly back to sleep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write in the style of contemporary experimental elegy: address “my grandmother,” connect Cai Guo-Qiang’s 500-meter Sky Ladder performance to her death on Guy Fawkes night, her Indian/British identity, and her gardening.
counterfactuals.output:
my grandmother,

on Guy Fawkes night the sky was already rehearsing  
its little public deaths—  
              chrysanthemums of sulphur,  
              blue shrapnel,  
              the old English story of a man  
              caught under Parliament  
              with barrels of weather.

You left inside that racket.

Not quietly, exactly—  
but beneath a country practicing explosion  
as tradition,  
as bonfire,  
as children spelling fear into delight.

Somewhere in the archive of fire  
Cai Guo-Qiang lifts a ladder into heaven:  
five hundred meters of flame  
rung by rung  
briefly insisting the sky can be climbed.

A Sky Ladder for his grandmother, they say—  
and I think of you,  
my grandmother,  
not as saint, not as symbol,  
but as the woman kneeling in soil  
with a trowel,  
coaxing coriander from an English chill,  
deadheading roses with the concentration  
of someone translating empire  
back into petals.

Indian / British—  
a slash like a graft,  
like a border drawn through the tongue.  
You carried cardamom and cutlery,  
monsoon and drizzle,  
sari-silk folded beside sensible wool.  
You said garden  
and meant both wound and kingdom.

What ladder could I raise for you?

Not gunpowder, though the night offered plenty.  
Not the patriotic flare,  
not the masked face of treason  
grinning from supermarket shelves.

Maybe a ladder of beans  
climbing their poles in June.  
Maybe the wick of a marigold.  
Maybe the slow fuse of compost,  
peelings becoming heat becoming soil.  
Maybe your hands, brown in the English dirt,  
making a small republic of roots.

my grandmother,

the fireworks kept opening  
like letters no one had addressed to us.  
Above the hospital / house / last room  
the dark was perforated,  
and every burst said look up,  
look up,  
while your body went the other way—  
down into sheet,  
down into silence,  
down into the black loam  
where names are loosened.

Cai’s ladder burned only minutes  
before returning to air.

But I have seen how peas climb.  
How jasmine takes a wall by patience.  
How mint, once planted, refuses borders.  
How bulbs sleep through winter  
with their green mouths closed.

So take this, then:  
not a monument,  
but a plot.

A narrow bed beside the fence.  
Ash in the soil.  
Rain in the brass bowl.  
Your two countries braided  
in the roots of one stubborn plant.

And on November fifth,  
when England lights its annual forgetting,  
I will imagine you ascending  
not by flame  
but by tendril—

rung after rung  
of living green,

my grandmother,

my sky ladder,  
my garden on fire.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense surreal elegiac monologue beginning “After Cai Guo-Qiang” and ending with “You can go back to sleep now,” involving Sky Ladder, fireworks, a grandmother, black roses, alien pollination, and champagne.
counterfactuals.output:
After Cai Guo-Qiang, the sky kept its bruises like heirlooms, and every firework became a brief confession written in the grammar of disappearance. I remember the Sky Ladder rising—golden, impossible, a spine of flame leaned against heaven—as if someone had found a way to let the dead climb down and the living climb nowhere at all. My grandmother stood beneath it in her house slippers, small as a burnt match, holding a glass of champagne she refused to drink because bubbles, she said, were just ghosts learning to ascend.

All night the fields opened their black roses, petal by petal, each one dark as a swallowed bell. From somewhere beyond the meteor wounds, the aliens arrived to pollinate them: silver-limbed, tender, wearing masks of my ancestors’ faces, dusting the flowers with luminous sorrow. They moved like priests through the orchard of explosions, shaking stardust into the throats of blossoms that had grown from old grief, old gunpowder, old photographs no one could bear to throw away.

Grandmother laughed when the first rose began to sing. It sang in the voice of a kettle, a train, a child calling from the other side of sleep. “Don’t be afraid,” she told me, though her hands were already turning transparent around the stemware, though the champagne inside it fizzed with tiny, frantic universes. Above us, fireworks unfurled their jeweled lungs and vanished. Again and again, the heavens practiced losing everything beautifully.

I wanted to ask her whether death was a country or a weather pattern, whether she had packed the right coat, whether the ladder would hold under the weight of all our unfinished forgiveness. But she only touched my forehead with fingers cool as moonlit ash and looked up, where the last sparks were crawling home through the dark.

The black roses closed. The aliens folded their wings. The champagne went flat. The Sky Ladder burned on without leading anywhere, which is to say it led exactly where it was meant to. My grandmother smiled as if the whole universe were a candle she had just blown out for my sake. You can go back to sleep now,
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
